data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference of truth, but as a non-inductive methodological rule grounded in the aim of science to increase verisimilitude (truth-likeness); accepting this costs the scientist any guarantee that the preferred theory is actually true or even probable, requiring a 'rational faith' in the method rather than the outcome.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If 'verisimilitude' is admitted to be unquantifiable and formally undefined (as Popper later conceded regarding his own definition), the mechanism loses its objective metric for preference.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the choice to act on the best-tested theory implicitly assumes the future will resemble the past (uniformity of nature), the distinction from Humean induction collapses.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'rational faith' in the method is indistinguishable in practice from pragmatic induction, the semantic separation is merely verbal.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'justification of belief' (which Popper rejects as inductive) and 'justification of action' (which he accepts as critical). By defining the goal of science as maximizing verisimilitude rather than probability, Popper argues that severe testing eliminates error, thereby increasing content without increasing logical probability. The preference is thus a rational choice to adopt the theory that has withstood the most rigorous attempts at falsification, as it is the best candidate for being closer to the truth, even if we can never know it is so.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
